learn.title: Notes for people
learn.body: A comment is text the compiler ignores. It is a note for human readers, including you next week. Good comments explain why code does something, not just what it does.

learn.title: Two kinds of comment
learn.body: `//` runs to the end of the line. `/* ... */` can span many lines.

learn.title: Pseudocode
learn.body: Pseudocode is a plan written in plain words before you write real code. For example: ask for a name, then greet that person. It helps you think about the steps without worrying about syntax.

learn.title: Compiler errors
learn.body: If your code breaks the rules, the compiler reports an error and builds nothing. The message shows the file, line number and a short reason. Read the first error first, because later ones are often caused by it.

learn.title: Fixing a missing semicolon
steps: The compiler says: error: expected ';' after expression
The message points at the line with `printf`
Add `;` at the end of that line and compile again

learn.body: Exact wording differs between clang and gcc, but the file, line and reason are always there.

questions.prompt: What does the compiler do with a comment?
questions.explanation: Comments are only for people reading the code.

questions.prompt: Which line starts a one-line comment in C?
questions.explanation: C uses `//` for one-line comments and `/* */` for longer ones.

questions.prompt: A comment that can span many lines starts with \_\_.
A plan written in plain words before coding is called \_\_.
questions.explanation: Pseudocode lets you plan the steps first.

questions.prompt: The compiler reports several errors. Which should you fix first?
questions.explanation: Later errors are often side effects of the first one.

questions.prompt: What character is usually missing when the compiler says expected ';'? Type it.
questions.explanation: The compiler expected a semicolon to end the instruction.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of fixing an error in order.
steps: Read the line number and message
questions.explanation: Read the message first, then fix, then check that it is gone.
A good comment tells the reader why, not just that something is here.
